learn.hook: You stand holding a heavy school bag for ten minutes and your arms ache. Yet a physicist says you did no work at all! What does 'work' really mean?
points: In science, work is done when a force moves an object. Work = force × displacement in the direction of the force: W = F × s.
The SI unit of work is the joule (J). 1 J of work is done when a force of 1 N moves an object by 1 m in its own direction.
No work is done if there is no displacement, or if the force is at right angles to the displacement. Work is negative when the force opposes the motion, like friction on a sliding box.
Power is the rate of doing work: P = W ÷ t. Its SI unit is the watt (W); 1 W = 1 J/s and 1 kW = 1000 W.
Electrical energy is sold in kilowatt-hours: 1 kWh = 1 'unit' = 3.6 × 10⁶ J.

example.q: Think it through: Ravi pushes a box with a force of 20 N and moves it 5 m along the floor in 10 s. How much work does he do, and what is his power?
steps: The force and the displacement are in the same direction.

learn.reallife: Your family's electricity bill counts 'units', and every unit is 1 kWh of energy. A 1000 W geyser running for one hour uses 1 unit.

games.title: Work done or not (in science)?
items: Lifting a bucket of water from a well
Pushing a cart along the road
A bullock pulling a plough across a field
Climbing the stairs to your classroom
Pushing hard against a wall that does not move
Holding a heavy bag still for ten minutes
Reading a book silently in a chair

items.q: Force 10 N moves an object 3 m (in the force's direction): work in J?
Force 50 N, displacement 2 m: work in J?
600 J of work in 20 s: power in W?
A 500 W iron used for 2 hours: energy in kWh?
Power 40 W for 5 s: work in J?

quiz.q: A force of 20 N moves a box 5 m in the direction of the force. How much work is done, in joules?
quiz.mistake: Divides force by distance instead of multiplying

quiz.q: A porter carries a suitcase on his head and walks along a level platform. How much work does he do against gravity on the suitcase?
options: Work equal to the suitcase's weight
quiz.explain: Gravity acts downwards but the suitcase moves horizontally, at right angles to the force, so no work is done against gravity.
quiz.mistake: Thinks feeling tired always means work is done in the scientific sense

quiz.q: A motor does 1500 J of work in 10 s. What is its power in watts?
quiz.mistake: Multiplies work and time instead of dividing

quiz.q: How many joules are there in 1 kWh?
quiz.mistake: Forgets to convert either kilowatts to watts or hours to seconds

quiz.q: A box slides across the floor and slows down. What kind of work does friction do on the box?
quiz.explain: Friction acts opposite to the direction of motion, so the work done by friction is negative.
quiz.mistake: Thinks all work is positive

quiz.q: Asha pushes against a wall with all her strength, but the wall does not move. How much work has she done on the wall?
options: A lot, because she pushed hard
quiz.explain: Work needs displacement. The wall did not move, so no work is done on it.
quiz.mistake: Equates effort or tiredness with work

quiz.q: A 100 W bulb is switched on for 10 hours. How many units (kWh) of electricity does it use?
quiz.explain: Energy = power × time = 100 W × 10 h = 1000 Wh = 1 kWh = 1 unit.
quiz.mistake: Forgets to divide by 1000 to change watt-hours to kilowatt-hours

quiz.q: What is the SI unit of power?
quiz.explain: Power is measured in watts; 1 W = 1 J/s. The kilowatt-hour is a unit of energy.
quiz.mistake: Confuses the unit of energy (kWh, joule) with the unit of power (watt)

teach.ask: Gappu holds a twig in his beak without moving: "My beak is SO tired. Surely I am doing a lot of work?"
teach.praise: Chirp! Work is force times displacement in the direction of the force. My twig did not move, so in science I did zero work, even though I feel tired!
teach.nudge: But did the twig actually move? What does work need besides a force?

learn.hook: Water stored high behind the Bhakra Nangal dam lights up homes in many states. How can water just sitting high up hold so much energy?
points: Energy is the capacity to do work. Its SI unit is the joule, the same as work.
Kinetic energy is the energy of motion: KE = ½mv². Doubling the speed makes the kinetic energy four times as large.
Potential energy is stored energy due to position or shape. Gravitational potential energy at height h is PE = mgh; a stretched rubber band or a bent bow has elastic potential energy.
Law of conservation of energy: energy can neither be created nor destroyed; it only changes from one form to another. The total energy stays the same.
For a freely falling object (ignoring air resistance), potential energy turns into kinetic energy, but their sum, the mechanical energy, stays constant.

example.q: Think it through: A 2 kg coconut falls from a height of 5 m. What is its potential energy at the top, and its kinetic energy just before it hits the ground? (Take g = 10 m/s² and ignore air resistance.)
steps: PE at the top = mgh = 2 × 10 × 5 = 100 J.
At the top it is at rest, so KE = 0.
As it falls, PE changes into KE, and the total stays 100 J.
Just before hitting the ground PE ≈ 0, so KE ≈ 100 J.
example.answer: PE at the top = 100 J; KE just before landing = 100 J.

learn.reallife: Hydroelectric dams change the potential energy of stored water into electricity, and the fun of a swing comes from KE and PE swapping back and forth.

games.title: Which energy is it?
pairs: A stretched bow just before release
Water stored high in a dam
Chemical energy changing to heat and light
A solar panel on a roof
Light energy changing to electrical energy

games.title: Energy changes at a hydroelectric plant
items: Water is stored high behind the dam (potential energy)
Water rushes down large pipes (kinetic energy)
Electricity reaches homes and lights bulbs

quiz.q: A 2 kg ball moves at 3 m/s. What is its kinetic energy in joules?
quiz.explain: KE = ½mv² = ½ × 2 × 3² = 9 J.
quiz.mistake: Forgets to square the speed, or forgets the ½

quiz.q: A 10 kg box is lifted onto a shelf 5 m high. What is its gain in potential energy, in joules? (Take g = 10 m/s².)
quiz.mistake: Leaves out g and multiplies only mass and height

quiz.q: If the speed of a scooter is doubled, its kinetic energy becomes
quiz.explain: KE depends on v². Doubling v makes v² four times bigger, so KE becomes four times as much.
quiz.mistake: Thinks KE is directly proportional to speed

quiz.q: A stretched catapult (gulel) has which kind of energy?
quiz.explain: Energy is stored in the stretched rubber because of its changed shape. That is elastic potential energy.
quiz.mistake: Thinks potential energy comes only from height

quiz.q: A mango falls from a tree. Ignoring air resistance, what happens to its energy as it falls?
options: Potential energy turns into kinetic energy, and the total stays constant
Both potential and kinetic energy increase
Kinetic energy turns into potential energy
quiz.explain: As height decreases, PE decreases and KE increases by the same amount, so the mechanical energy stays constant.
quiz.mistake: Thinks energy is lost or created during the fall

quiz.q: A ball is thrown straight up. At its highest point, what is its kinetic energy?
quiz.explain: At the highest point the ball stops for an instant, so v = 0 and KE = 0. All its energy is potential energy then.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the ball has most kinetic energy at the top

quiz.q: Which statement is the law of conservation of energy?
options: Energy can be created by machines
Energy is always lost as heat and disappears
Energy can neither be created nor destroyed, only changed from one form to another
Energy and force are the same thing
quiz.explain: Energy only changes form. The total amount of energy in a closed system stays the same.
quiz.mistake: Thinks machines can create energy

quiz.q: A 2 kg coconut falls from a height of 5 m. What is its kinetic energy just before it hits the ground, in joules? (g = 10 m/s², ignore air resistance.)
quiz.explain: All the starting PE (mgh = 2 × 10 × 5 = 100 J) has changed into KE just before landing.
quiz.mistake: Thinks kinetic energy is zero just because the coconut started at rest

teach.ask: Gappu sits on a swing: "I go up, I go down, up, down! Where does my energy go each time?"
teach.praise: Tweet tweet! At the top I have potential energy, at the bottom kinetic energy, and they keep changing into each other while the total stays the same!
teach.nudge: At the very top of the swing I stop for a moment. What kind of energy do I have there?

learn.hook: How does a small child lift a heavy friend on a see-saw, and how is a heavy bucket raised from a village well with ease? Simple machines!
points: A lever is a rigid bar that turns about a fixed point called the fulcrum. The force we apply is the effort, and the weight lifted is the load.
Principle of the lever: load × load arm = effort × effort arm. Mechanical advantage (MA) = load ÷ effort.

First-class lever: fulcrum between effort and load (see-saw, scissors, beam balance). Second-class: load between fulcrum and effort (wheelbarrow, nutcracker, bottle opener). Third-class: effort between fulcrum and load (fire tongs, fishing rod, human forearm).
A single fixed pulley does not reduce the effort (MA = 1) but changes its direction, so you can pull down to lift up, as at a well or a flagpole.
A single movable pulley ideally has MA = 2, so the effort is half the load. Combinations of pulleys (block and tackle) are used in cranes.

example.q: Think it through: A load of 200 N sits 0.5 m from the fulcrum of a crowbar. The effort is applied 2 m from the fulcrum on the other side. What effort is needed?
steps: Principle of the lever: load × load arm = effort × effort arm.

learn.reallife: The hand pump in a village, a pair of scissors, the nutcracker (sarota) for supari and the crane at a construction site are all simple machines.

items.text: In a first-class lever, the ___ is between the effort and the load.
A single fixed pulley has a mechanical advantage of ___.
An ideal single movable pulley has a mechanical advantage of ___.

quiz.q: A see-saw is which class of lever?
quiz.explain: The fulcrum (pivot) of a see-saw lies between the effort and the load, so it is a first-class lever.
quiz.mistake: Does not identify the position of the fulcrum

quiz.q: In a wheelbarrow, the load is between the wheel (fulcrum) and the handles (effort). Which class of lever is it?
quiz.explain: When the load is between the fulcrum and the effort, the lever is second class.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up the definitions of second- and third-class levers

quiz.q: Which of these is a third-class lever?
quiz.explain: In a fishing rod the effort (the front hand) is between the fulcrum (the hand at the end) and the load (the fish).
quiz.mistake: Classifies levers by what they look like instead of where the effort is

quiz.q: A 200 N load is 0.5 m from the fulcrum. The effort arm is 2 m. What effort is needed, in newtons?
quiz.explain: Load × load arm = effort × effort arm, so 200 × 0.5 = effort × 2, giving effort = 50 N.
quiz.mistake: Multiplies instead of dividing by the effort arm

quiz.q: A machine lifts a 300 N load when an effort of 100 N is applied. What is its mechanical advantage?
quiz.explain: MA = load ÷ effort = 300 ÷ 100 = 3.
quiz.mistake: Divides effort by load

quiz.q: Why is a single fixed pulley used at a village well, even though it does not reduce the effort?
options: It changes the direction of the effort, so you can pull down to lift up
quiz.explain: Pulling down is easier and safer because you can use your body weight. A fixed pulley has MA = 1 but changes the direction of force.
quiz.mistake: Thinks every machine must reduce the effort

quiz.q: What is the ideal mechanical advantage of a single movable pulley?
quiz.explain: Two parts of the rope share the load, so ideally the effort is half the load and MA = 2.
quiz.mistake: Confuses a movable pulley with a fixed pulley (MA = 1)

quiz.q: Your forearm is a third-class lever with MA less than 1. What is its advantage?
options: It needs less effort than the load
A small movement of the muscle makes the hand move a long way quickly
quiz.explain: Third-class levers need more effort than the load, but they give a gain in speed and distance of movement.
quiz.mistake: Thinks a lever is useful only if it reduces effort

teach.ask: Gappu wants to lift a big seed with a twig: "Where should I put the pebble under my twig so lifting is easiest?"
teach.praise: Chirp chirp! Put the fulcrum close to the load so the effort arm is long. Then a small effort lifts a big load. Load × load arm = effort × effort arm!
teach.nudge: Should the pebble (fulcrum) be close to the seed or close to my beak? Why?
